title: Amazon Revenue Hits $201 Billion as AWS Posts Fastest Growth in 18 Quarters
excerpt: Cloud unit revenue surged 37% to $42.2 billion, beating estimates by a wide margin, as Amazon raised its 2026 capex outlook to $220 billion.
body:
• Amazon reported Q2 revenue of $201 billion, up 20% year-over-year and beating Wall Street's $197 billion estimate.
  • AWS revenue surged 37% to $42.2 billion — its fastest growth in 18 quarters — driven by booming AI and cloud demand.
  • The company raised its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $220 billion, up from $200 billion, as AI infrastructure spending accelerates.
  • Shares jumped as much as 10% after hours, even as free cash flow turned negative for the second straight quarter at -$7.6 billion.

AWS Delivers a Blowout Quarter

Amazon crushed Wall Street expectations on Thursday, posting quarterly revenue of $201 billion and signaling that demand for artificial intelligence services remains strong enough to justify its massive infrastructure buildout. Shares surged as much as 10% in after-hours trading.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=7hC6-dYK1rQ

The star of the report was Amazon Web Services, which posted revenue growth of 37% to $42.2 billion — well ahead of the 31% growth analysts had forecast and the cloud unit's fastest expansion in 18 quarters.

"AWS is booming."

— Andy Jassy, Amazon CEO

Jassy noted that AWS's AI and custom chip businesses have each surpassed annualized run rates of more than $25 billion, underscoring the scale of enterprise demand for cloud-based AI services. The unit posted an operating margin of 39%, well above analyst consensus.

A $220 Billion Spending Bet

Amazon announced it would increase its 2026 capital expenditure guidance to $220 billion, up 10% from its prior forecast of $200 billion and a staggering 72% increase over last year's $128 billion. The bulk of the spending is directed at AWS data centers, generative AI infrastructure, and custom silicon.

The company spent $53.1 billion on capex in Q2 alone, eclipsing operating cash flow and pushing trailing 12-month free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion — the second consecutive quarter of cash burn. A year earlier, Amazon generated $18.2 billion in free cash flow over the same period.

Unlike recent capex announcements from Alphabet and Meta Platforms that spooked investors, Amazon's spending hike was received warmly. Barron's reported that shares actually took another leg up in after-hours trading following the capex update, a sign investors trust the demand backing the investment.

AI Demand Outpacing Supply

The results mirror strong cloud performances from Microsoft and Alphabet earlier this week, but AWS's growth rate is now getting closer to its smaller competitors — a notable shift after years of deceleration. The company has raised prices on AI server rentals twice this year, most recently a month ago, suggesting demand continues to outstrip available capacity.

AWS has built a roster of major partnerships in 2026, including cloud infrastructure and chip supply deals with OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta Platforms, Pinterest, and Snowflake. Amazon's CFO said the company's AI and chips businesses were growing at rates that justified continued aggressive investment.

Earnings Boosted by Anthropic Stake

Earnings per share came in at $5.75, dwarfing last year's $1.68 and smashing the Wall Street consensus of $1.82. The outsized figure was helped by $53 billion in non-operational income, primarily an unrealized gain on Amazon's stake in privately held AI lab Anthropic.

On the retail side, Jassy said Amazon set record delivery speeds for Prime members in the first half of the year, with 40% more items delivered same-day or overnight compared to the prior year. The company also received approximately $600 million in tariff refunds during Q2, though the impact was limited by forward-buying and pre-positioning of inventory.

What to Watch

The key question going forward is whether AWS's torrid growth can be sustained as competition from Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud intensifies. Both rivals are investing heavily in their own AI infrastructure and enterprise offerings. For investors with exposure to U.S. tech — including many in the Indian diaspora — Amazon's results offer reassurance that the AI spending cycle is generating real returns, not just promises.
